summary: Defines an additional Cryptographic Message Syntax content type, authenticated-enveloped-data, for use with authenticated encryption modes. It supports the same key management techniques as the existing enveloped-data type. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5083 defines a CMS message format that encrypts content and lets recipients check whether it was changed. Each recipient gets an encrypted copy of the content key, and the recipient must verify the message before using its plaintext.

subtitle: A CMS content type that encrypts content and authenticates it in one operation.

tldr.problem: CMS needs a content type designed for authenticated-encryption algorithms, which encrypt data and check its integrity together.
tldr.mechanism: The sender encrypts content with a randomly generated key, authenticates optional unencrypted attributes, and encrypts a copy of the content key for each recipient.
tldr.outcome: Recipients must verify integrity before releasing plaintext. RFC 5083 updates RFC 3852.

today: RFC 5083 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2007 and updates RFC 3852. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: A Content Type for Authenticated Encryption
sections.content:
The authenticated-enveloped-data content type is intended for authenticated-encryption algorithms. It can carry content of any type and attributes that are authenticated but not encrypted.

It supports the key management techniques available to the CMS enveloped-data content type. The format uses ASN.1 and the BER and DER encoding rules; companion RFC 5084 describes conventions for AES-CCM and AES-GCM.
sections.plainLanguage: This CMS format combines encryption with an integrity check. It can also protect selected attributes without hiding them.

sections.title: Building and Opening an Envelope
sections.content:
The sender generates a random content-authenticated-encryption key and encrypts that key separately for each recipient. The sender collects recipient information, authenticated attributes, encrypted content, the authentication result, and any unprotected attributes into an AuthEnvelopedData value.

A recipient decrypts one copy of the content key, then decrypts and verifies the content and authenticated attributes. Integrity must be checked before information, especially plaintext, is released. If the check fails, all plaintext must be destroyed.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender uses one random key for the content and prepares a protected copy of that key for each recipient. A recipient must check the integrity result before revealing the decrypted content.

sections.title: Fields in AuthEnvelopedData
sections.content:
The content type is identified by id-ct-authEnvelopedData, and its ASN.1 type is AuthEnvelopedData. The version field must be 0, recipientInfos must contain at least one recipient, and authEncryptedContentInfo carries the protected content.

Optional authAttrs hold authenticated attributes and must be DER encoded when present. The mac field contains the integrity value produced by the authenticated-encryption algorithm. Optional unauthAttrs are not protected.
sections.plainLanguage: The structure separates recipient key information, protected content, authenticated notes, and unprotected notes. The recipient must not treat unprotected notes as verified.

sections.title: Encrypting Content and Attributes
sections.content:
The authenticated-encryption algorithm receives the content, the key, and the authenticated attributes encoded as additional authenticated data. If the algorithm needs padding, CMS padding rules apply and are defined for block sizes below 256 octets.

The encrypted content is stored as an OCTET STRING and the authentication tag is stored in mac. If there are no authenticated attributes, the algorithm receives zero bits of additional authenticated data.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm encrypts the content and computes an authentication tag from the content and any authenticated attributes. The format stores the encrypted bytes and tag in separate fields.

sections.title: Four Ways to Deliver a Content Key
sections.content:
For each recipient, the sender may use key transport, key agreement, a previously distributed symmetric key-encryption key, or a password-derived key-encryption key. Different recipients of the same content may use different techniques.

Only the content key is input to each recipient's key-encryption process. Recipient-specific information is collected in RecipientInfo values.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS can protect the content key in four ways, including a recipient's public key, a shared secret, or a password-derived key. The method can differ from one recipient to another.

sections.title: Key and Nonce Safety
sections.content:
Implementations must generate content keys, padding, and unpredictable nonce values randomly. Reusing counter blocks with the same key can reuse a keystream and remove confidentiality, so a fresh content key can be generated for each content.

The message-digest attribute should not be included in authAttrs because it exposes an unencrypted hash that can support tracking or guesses about plaintext. The RFC also notes that encrypted messages limit defenses that inspect message text.
sections.plainLanguage: Random values and fresh keys matter because reusing encryption material can expose content. An unencrypted digest can also reveal clues about the message, so the RFC advises against including it.
